\chapter{One to Five, By the Road Urdu Did Not Borrow}
\label{ch:ur-count-five}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say, hear, read and write the Urdu numbers one to five, name the English cousin of each, and say why none of them came in from Persian.}

Five numbers, five Indo-European roots, no new letter and no Persian borrowing -- retrieved shuffled rather than recited.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ek]{\ur{ایک} — one, and the road this book keeps calling the other one}

\label{lesson:UR-C28-ek}



\begin{quote}
Name the two roads a word can take into Urdu: inherited from Sanskrit through Prakrit, or borrowed from Persian.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ایک}} — \emph{ek} — \textbf{one}
\end{quote}

Twenty-two chapters, and not one number. That has a price the book has been paying in silence: no age, no cost, no telephone number, no quantity, no time. It stops here.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{ایک}} continues Sanskrit \emph{eka} through Prakrit, from Indo-European *\emph{oywos}, \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} — the root behind English \textbf{one}, Latin \textbf{ūnus} and Greek \textbf{oîos}.

This book has spent chapters on words that came the OTHER way: \emph{garmī} and \emph{sardī} are Persian borrowings, sitting in Urdu beside inherited words that mean much the same. Numbers are where that stopped. Persian's \textbf{yek} was as available as Persian's \textbf{sard} was, and Urdu declined it — every one of the first ten numbers is the inherited form.

That is worth holding on to, because it makes the whole count predictable in one direction: if you know a Sanskrit or Hindi number you already know the Urdu one, and if you know only the Persian one you do not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ek} — one
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{ek} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{eka} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{oywos} $\to$ English \textbf{one}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} Persian \emph{yek} is the same root by a different road, and Urdu did not borrow it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%A7\%DB\%8C\%DA\%A9}{Wiktionary: \ur{ایک}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[do]{\ur{دو} — two, and a spelling that has been hiding in plain sight}

\label{lesson:UR-C28-do}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{ek} and which road it came by. Then say \emph{friend}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{دو}} — \emph{do} — \textbf{two}
\end{quote}

Two letters, and both of them have been on the page since the friend lesson — they open \emph{dost}, \textquotedblleft{}friend\textquotedblright{}. A search of this whole book for \textbf{\ur{دو}} finds it twice and both times inside \emph{dost}, which is exactly why a machine could report the word as present when the number had never been taught.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{دو}} continues Sanskrit \emph{dvi} through Prakrit \textbf{do}, from Indo-European *\emph{dwóh\textsubscript{1}}, \textquotedblleft{}two.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{two}, Latin \textbf{duo} and Greek \textbf{dýo} are the same word.

Say \emph{do} and \emph{two} one after the other. Nothing there has to be learned; it has to be recognised.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{do} — two
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{do} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{dvi} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{dwóh\textsubscript{1}} $\to$ English \textbf{two}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{ek, do}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AF\%D9\%88}{Wiktionary: \ur{دو}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tīn]{\ur{تین} — three, and how much of a word a language can keep}

\label{lesson:UR-C28-teen}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{do} and its English cousin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{تین}} — \emph{tīn} — \textbf{three}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{تین}} continues Sanskrit \emph{tri}, from Indo-European *\emph{treyes}, \textquotedblleft{}three.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{three}, Latin \textbf{trēs} and Greek \textbf{treîs} are the same word.

Now set it beside the Persian for three, \emph{se}. Both descend from *\emph{treyes}. Urdu's form still has the \emph{t}; Persian's has lost the \emph{t} AND the \emph{r}, leaving one syllable. Same root, two roads, and one of them wore the word down much further.

An English speaker hears \emph{tīn} and gets \textbf{three} for nothing. Hearing \emph{se} as \textbf{three} takes a moment.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{tīn} — three
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{tīn} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{tri} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{treyes} $\to$ English \textbf{three}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{ek, do, tīn}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AA\%DB\%8C\%D9\%86}{Wiktionary: \ur{تین}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chār]{\ur{چار} — four, and one consonant's three fates}

\label{lesson:UR-C28-char}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{tīn}, say which sound it keeps that Persian lost, then say \textbf{do}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{چار}} — \emph{chār} — \textbf{four}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{چار}} continues Sanskrit \emph{catvāraḥ}, from Indo-European *\emph{k\textsuperscript{w}etwóres}, \textquotedblleft{}four.\textquotedblright{}

The opening *\emph{k\textsuperscript{w}} is where this gets interesting, because three branches did three different things with it. Latin kept it whole: \textbf{quattuor}. English lost the lip-rounding and softened the \emph{k} to \emph{f}: \textbf{four}. Indo-Aryan pushed it forward to a \textbf{ch}, which is what you are saying.

One sound, three descendants, and the numbers still line up.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{chār} — four
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{chār} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{catvāraḥ} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{kwetwores} $\to$ Latin \textbf{quattuor}, English \textbf{four}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{ek, do, tīn, chār}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DA\%86\%D8\%A7\%D8\%B1}{Wiktionary: \ur{چار}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pānch]{\ur{پانچ} — five, and a word you have met on a map}

\label{lesson:UR-C28-panch}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{chār}, and what three languages did with the sound it starts from.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{پانچ}} — \emph{pānch} — \textbf{five}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{\ur{ن}} in the middle is nasalising the vowel before it rather than standing as a full \emph{n} of its own — the behaviour this book named several chapters ago.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{پانچ}} continues Sanskrit \emph{pañca}, from Indo-European *\emph{pénk\textsuperscript{w}e}, \textquotedblleft{}five.\textquotedblright{} Greek \textbf{pénte}, Latin \textbf{quīnque} and English \textbf{five} are the same word.

An English speaker has almost certainly met it already without being told. \textbf{Punjab} is \emph{panj} + \emph{āb}, \textquotedblleft{}five waters\textquotedblright{} — the land of the five rivers — and the fruit drink \textbf{punch} is named for its five ingredients. The number was in the reader's language before this lesson was.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{pānch} — five
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{pānch} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{pañca} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{penkwe} $\to$ Greek \textbf{pénte}, English \textbf{five}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{ek, do, tīn, chār, pānch} — the whole first five
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%BE\%D8\%A7\%D9\%86\%DA\%86}{Wiktionary: \ur{پانچ}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — one to five, out of order}

\label{lesson:UR-C28-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{pānch}, then \textbf{ek}, then which of the two roads both came by.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A run learned forwards is a rhyme. Break it four ways.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Hear each of the five named singly and out of order, and say what it is.
  \item Count backwards from \textbf{pānch} to \textbf{ek}.
  \item Read the five printed shuffled — \textbf{\ur{پانچ،} \ur{ایک،} \ur{چار،} \ur{تین،} \ur{دو}} — and say each.
  \item Write all five from dictation. Every letter in all five has been on the page for chapters; the tranche adds no new sign at all.
\end{enumerate}

Then say each number's English cousin: \textbf{one, two, three, four, five}. All five have one, and that is not a coincidence — it is the same set of words, five thousand years apart, arriving by the inherited road rather than the Persian one.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
